read.sections.0.text.back: For most of human history, people got food by foraging. They gathered wild plants, hunted animals and caught fish. More than 10,000 years ago, some groups started planting seeds and keeping animals. Farming did not start in just one place or at just one time, and each part of the world grew different crops. Farmers in West Asia grew wheat and barley, while farmers in China grew rice and millet. People on the island of Papua (New Guinea) grew bananas and taro, and people in Mexico grew maize and beans. People in the Andes Mountains were the first to grow potatoes, and people in parts of Africa were the first to grow sorghum. In Harapan Valley, one group still moves around to look for food, while the other group farms.
read.sections.0.text.source: For most of human history, people got their food by foraging. They gathered wild plants, hunted animals and caught fish. More than 10,000 years ago, some groups began to plant seeds and keep animals. Farming did not start in just one place or at one time, and different parts of the world grew different crops. Farmers in West Asia grew wheat and barley, while farmers in China grew rice and millet. People in New Guinea grew bananas and taro, and people in Mexico grew maize and beans. People in the Andes mountains first farmed potatoes, and people in parts of Africa first farmed sorghum. In Harapan Valley, one group still moves around to find food, while the other group farms.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Extra food changed work and trade

read.sections.1.text.back: Farming can produce a lot of food on a small piece of land. After a good harvest, a village might have a surplus, that is, more food than people need at that time. Because there was stored grain, not everyone had to farm, so some people could specialise in making pots, cloth or tools. In Harapan Valley, one family makes clay pots and gives them to farmers in exchange for grain. This is one form of trade. Villages also traded with each other, and a village near the sea might exchange salt for grain. Over time, some farming villages grew into towns.
read.sections.1.text.source: Farming could grow a lot of food in a small area. After a good harvest, a village might have a surplus, which is more food than people need right away. With extra grain in store, not everyone had to farm, so some people could specialise in making pots, cloth or tools. In Harapan Valley, one family makes clay pots and gives them to farmers in exchange for grain. This is a kind of trade. Villages also traded with each other, and a village near the sea might trade salt for grain. Over time, some farming villages grew into towns.

read.sections.1.simpler.back: Fields can produce a lot of food in a small place. After a good harvest, there may be a surplus, or extra food. People store it for later. Now not everyone has to farm. So some people can specialise. They have one main job, like making pots. In Harapan Valley, one family makes pots. They give pots and get grain. This is trade. Villages also trade with each other. Some villages grow into towns.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: A farm can grow lots of food in a small space. After a good year, there may be a surplus of extra food. People keep it safe for later. Now not everyone has to farm, so some people can specialise. They do one main job, like making pots. In Harapan Valley, one family makes pots. They give pots and get grain. This is trade. Villages trade with each other too, and some grow into towns.

read.sections.2.text.back: Farming is hard work, with long days of planting, watering and harvesting. Many villages depended on only a few kinds of crops. If the rain didn't fall, the harvest could fail and people had only a little food. Living close to animals and to many other people also made some diseases spread more easily. In some places, a handful of families controlled more land and stored grain, so they had more power. Not every group chose to farm, and many kept foraging or did both. So historians ask a question carefully: was farming better, and better for whom?
read.sections.2.text.source: Farming was hard work, with long days of planting, watering and harvesting. Many villages depended on only a few crops. If the rain did not come, the harvest could fail and people had little to eat. Living close to animals and to many other people also helped some illnesses spread. In some places, a few families took control of more land and stored grain, which gave them more power. Not every group chose to farm, and many kept foraging or did some of both. So historians ask a careful question: was farming better, and better for whom?

read.sections.2.simpler.back: Farming is hard work. Many villages only grew a few kinds of crops. If the rain didn't fall, the plants could die. Then food became scarce. People lived close to animals and to other people. So diseases could spread. Some families got more land and food. This gave them more power. Not all groups chose to farm. Many kept foraging. So we ask: is farming better? Better for whom?

People live close to animals and to each other, so sickness can spread. Some families get more land and food. This gives them more power. Not every group chooses to farm. Many keep foraging. So we ask: was farming better? Who was it better for?

write.example.back: Farming helped people because it could produce a lot of food in one place. One example from the lesson is the farming village in Harapan Valley. After a good harvest, the village had a grain surplus. Because of that, one family could specialise in making pots. But farming also brought problems: the village only grew a few kinds of crops. If the rain didn't fall, the whole harvest could fail. This was hard for families who had no land or extra grain. So, I think farming was important, but it was not better for everyone.

watch.summary.back: This video explains why farming was a very big change in human history. For a very long time, people looked for food in the wild. Then people in some parts of the world started growing crops and keeping animals. Farming could produce more food on smaller land. So more people could live in one place, and villages could grow. Stored food let some people do other work, like making tools or trading. Some people became leaders. Farming also changed the land around people. But farming also brought risks. A bad harvest could mean hunger/famine. Diseases could spread more easily. Some people got much more land and power than others. Farming was very important, but it did not make everyone's life better in the same way.
watch.summary.source: This video explains why farming was such a big change in human history. For a very long time, people found their food in the wild. Then people in several parts of the world began to grow crops and keep animals. Farming could make more food in a smaller area. So more people could live in one place, and villages could grow. Stored food let some people do other work, like making tools or trading. Some people became leaders. Farming also changed the land around people. But farming brought risks too. A bad harvest could mean hunger. Illness could spread more easily. Some people got much more land and power than others. Farming was very important, but it did not make life better for everyone in the same way.
